saints.sourceTitle: Saint John [Maximovitch], Archbishop of Shanghai and San Francisco

summary.text: John Maximovitch is remembered as a ROCOR bishop whose ministry extended through China, Western Europe, and North America. The OCA page records his repose on June 19 Old Style / July 2 New Style in 1966, ROCOR glorification in 1994, and subsequent recognition by Moscow in 2008. The page credits the Monastery of Saint John for its life. His commemoration therefore requires particular care about calendar labels.

blocks.text: John Maximovitch was born Michael in 1896 and was educated in the Russian Empire before his family’s emigration. In Serbia he completed theological study, became a monk and priest, and taught before being consecrated Bishop of Shanghai in 1934.

blocks.text: In Shanghai he cared for abandoned children and helped complete the cathedral. After the communist takeover in 1949, he accompanied Russian refugees through Hong Kong to the Philippines. He later served in San Francisco from 1962 until his death.

blocks.text: A recollection published by ROCOR comes from Archbishop Peter, who knew John personally and accompanied him as an acolyte. He remembers visits to sick people, attention to the dead, a sense of humor, and a pocket watch given by an orphan. He also distinguishes a genuine orphanage from a simplified legend: some children stayed long-term, while others were taken in temporarily when a parent was hospitalized.

blocks.text: The Chinese Orthodox historical account locates his arrival in Shanghai in 1934, following consecration in Belgrade. It connects his care for abandoned children with the completion of the cathedral dedicated to the Mother of God, Surety of Sinners. The orphanage’s later icon history records evacuation from China through the Philippines and onward to San Francisco.

blocks.text: Priest Dionisy Pozdnyaev’s history places John’s charitable work within the refugee institutions of Shanghai. It cites a letter to Metropolitan Meletius describing two hundred children at the Saint Tikhon of Zadonsk orphanage, improved care at the Saint Philaret charity home, and hospital visits by priests. It also records John’s part in founding a Chinese Orthodox Brotherhood in June 1935, intended to bring Chinese Christians and Russian emigrants together. The brotherhood promoted study in both languages. His concern extended beyond preserving a Russian refugee community to the establishment of an Orthodox Church among Chinese people.
